genre/popsong-rock-en-compilatiescore.text: In the late 1960s, filmmakers discovered that existing pop songs could carry a film. In The Graduate (1967), Mike Nichols used songs by Simon & Garfunkel. Easy Rider (1969) had no composed score but a string of rock tracks, among them Steppenwolf. For Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (1969), Burt Bacharach wrote the airy ‘Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head’. In American Graffiti (1973), the radio plays hits from the 1950s and early 1960s throughout the film. Quentin Tarantino built Pulp Fiction (1994) on surf rock and soul from his own record collection. The soundtrack album thus became an important commercial product as well.
genre/popsong-rock-en-compilatiescore.listen: Notice how an existing song takes on a different meaning because it plays under particular images.

genre/postpunk.text: Post-punk kept the energy and do-it-yourself attitude of punk but let go of the three chords. Joy Division from Manchester released their records on the local label Factory; in New York, Talking Heads showed that rock could be nervous, ironic and danceable. After the death of Ian Curtis in 1980, Joy Division carried on as New Order.
genre/postpunk.listen: In She's Lost Control, hear how the bass plays the melody while the drums sound dry and almost mechanical.

genre/powerpop.text: Power pop is guitar pop with the melodies and harmony singing of the early Beatles and the force of loud guitars. In the early 1970s it was played by Badfinger, Raspberries and Big Star, followed later by Cheap Trick and The Knack. In 1994, Weezer made a declaration of love to the 1950s with Buddy Holly, played on heavily distorted guitars: power pop for the alternative rock generation.
genre/powerpop.listen: In Buddy Holly, hear the cheerful pop melody on top of a wall of distorted guitars.

genre/prehistorische-muziek.text: In caves in the Swabian Jura, in southern Germany, archaeologists found flutes made of swan bone, vulture bone and mammoth ivory. The finds from the Geißenklösterle cave are about 42,000 years old and are among the oldest musical instruments in the world. They were made by the first modern humans in Europe, who also carved figurines in the same caves. Nobody knows what their music sounded like, but reconstructed flutes show which notes were already possible then.
genre/prehistorische-muziek.listen: This is a modern improvisation on a reconstructed Ice Age flute, not a surviving melody. Hear how few notes the instrument has, and how the player still builds a melody with breath and repetition.

genre/prestige-tv-en-streaming.text: Around 2000, cable channels such as HBO, and later streaming services, began making series with the budget and ambition of feature films. As a result, music gained more space and time. Bear McCreary gave Battlestar Galactica (2004) a score full of percussion and non-Western instruments. Ramin Djawadi, who learned his trade in Hans Zimmer's team, wrote a title theme for Game of Thrones (2011) for cello over a constantly repeated rhythm. Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein made Stranger Things (2016) with analogue synthesizers in the spirit of the 1980s. In Succession (2018), Nicholas Britell set classical piano and strings over a hip hop beat. Natalie Holt used the theremin in Loki (2021). Title music became the hallmark of a series once again.
genre/prestige-tv-en-streaming.listen: Listen to the title music: which instrument carries the melody, and which element makes the series recognisable within a few seconds?

genre/progressieve-rock.text: Progressive rock turned the album into a composition, with long songs, classical influences and complicated time signatures. Close to the Edge (1972) by Yes fills an entire album side, and The Dark Side of the Moon (1973) by Pink Floyd is one continuous work. In the Netherlands, Focus broke through with prog rock with a sense of humour.
genre/progressieve-rock.listen: Count along in Money: the song is in seven beats, except during the guitar solo, with a tape loop of cash-register sounds as its rhythm.

genre/psalmen-en-tempelzang.text: According to the biblical Books of Chronicles, Levites sang and played in the Temple in Jerusalem, with lyres, harps, cymbals and trumpets, and the psalms were their songbook. After the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE, that music was lost. The chanted reading of the Bible and the blowing of the shofar, a ram's horn, did live on in the synagogue. That way of singing also became a source for early Christian chant.
genre/psalmen-en-tempelzang.listen: Hear how Yemenite Jews sing the Hallel psalms at the Passover meal: a cantor and a group, using the same short melodic formulas again and again. That community lived in isolation for centuries, but nobody knows for certain how close this is to Temple chant.

genre/psychedelische-rock.text: Around 1966 and 1967, bands drew inspiration from Indian music, the classical avant-garde and LSD. You hear drones, modal sounds and studio effects; the Beatles used tape loops and sounds played backwards. San Francisco, with the Summer of Love of 1967, and London were the centres.
genre/psychedelische-rock.listen: In White Rabbit, hear the march rhythm that keeps getting louder, with a Spanish, Phrygian sound.

genre/punk.text: Punk was the answer to rock that had become big, expensive and complicated: short, fast, loud songs with few chords and the idea that anyone can start a band. The Ramones played at the New York club CBGB; in London there were the Sex Pistols and The Clash. Bands released records on small labels and fans made fanzines.
genre/punk.listen: In Anarchy in the UK, hear the wall of guitars recorded over one another several times.

genre/purcell-handel-en-het-oratorium.text: In London, English and Italian music came together. Around 1689, Henry Purcell wrote Dido and Aeneas, a short opera that ends with Dido's lament over a constantly repeated bass line. The German George Frideric Handel settled in London in 1712 and composed Italian operas and the Water Music for a boat trip of King George I. When opera went out of fashion, he wrote English oratorios; Messiah premiered in Dublin in 1742.
genre/purcell-handel-en-het-oratorium.listen: In Dido's Lament, hear how the same descending bass line keeps returning while the voice sings freely above it.

genre/qawwali.text: Qawwali is the devotional singing of the Sufis in South Asia, performed at the tombs of saints. The tradition goes back to the poet Amir Khusrau, a disciple of the Sufi master Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi around 1300. One or two lead singers improvise, a chorus repeats their lines and claps its hands, harmonium and tabla accompany, and the tempo rises towards ecstasy. From 1985, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan of Pakistan brought qawwali to Western stages, beginning at the WOMAD festival.
genre/qawwali.listen: In Allah-hoo, hear how the Sabri Brothers repeat a single word endlessly and how the handclaps of the chorus give the rhythm ever more force.

genre/radiophonic-workshop.text: From 1958, the BBC had its own department for electronic sound, the Radiophonic Workshop, which made sounds and music for radio and television. In 1963, Delia Derbyshire built the Doctor Who theme, composed by Ron Grainer, note by note from oscillators, noise and tape loops. The staff worked anonymously.
genre/radiophonic-workshop.listen: The Doctor Who bass line is made from a single plucked string, cut again and again at a different pitch.

genre/raga-rock.text: In the mid-1960s, Western bands began to use Indian instruments and scales: raga rock. George Harrison played sitar on Norwegian Wood (1965) by The Beatles and later took lessons from Ravi Shankar; The Byrds and The Rolling Stones, with Paint It Black (1966), also used the sound. Long drones and modal melodies became a hallmark of psychedelic rock.
genre/raga-rock.listen: In Norwegian Wood, hear how the sitar follows the melody of the acoustic guitar.

genre/ragtime.text: Ragtime was the first African American style of music to be sold on a large scale as sheet music. The left hand plays a march bass, the right hand syncopations against the beat, and the form consists of strains of sixteen bars. Scott Joplin's Maple Leaf Rag was published in Sedalia, Missouri, in 1899.
genre/ragtime.listen: Listen for the difference between the steady march bass in the left hand and the syncopations in the right hand.

genre/rai.text: Raï comes from Oran in Algeria, where singers in cafés and at parties sang folk songs about love, drink and life, subjects that did not fit in traditional music. In the 1980s, synthesizers, drum machines and electric guitars were added: pop raï. Singers were given the title Cheb, ‘young man’; Cheb Khaled became the best known and also scored a hit in Europe with Didi (1992).
genre/rai.listen: In Didi, hear the synthesizers and the drum machine beneath the Arabic singing with its long ornaments.

genre/rave.text: In 1987, English DJs came back from Ibiza and began acid house nights in clubs; the summers of 1988 and 1989 became the Second Summer of Love. Parties moved to warehouses and fields, until a law in 1994 gave the police the right to shut them down. Jungle, drum and bass, big beat and IDM came out of rave.
genre/rave.listen: In Pump Up the Volume, hear how a track is built from dozens of samples of other records.

genre/rebetiko.text: Rebetiko is the music of the Greek port districts, above all Piraeus near Athens. After 1922, more than a million Greek refugees came to Greece from Asia Minor, present-day Turkey, bringing their café music full of Eastern scales. In the 1930s, Markos Vamvakaris made the bouzouki, a long-necked lute, the principal instrument. The songs are about poverty, love, prison and hashish. After the war, Vassilis Tsitsanis made rebetiko popular throughout Greece.
genre/rebetiko.listen: In Frangosyriani, hear the clear, plucked bouzouki and the calm dance rhythm of the hasapiko, an old Greek dance.

genre/reggaeton.text: Reggaeton grew in the 1990s in Panama and Puerto Rico out of Jamaican dancehall and hip hop, in Spanish. Its basis is the dembow rhythm, named after Dem Bow (1990) by Shabba Ranks: a stomping bass drum with a snare that falls just before and on the beat. In 2004, Daddy Yankee scored a worldwide hit with Gasolina, and Despacito (2017) by Luis Fonsi and Daddy Yankee became one of the most streamed songs ever.
genre/reggaeton.listen: In Gasolina, hear the dembow rhythm: the bass drum on every beat and the snare that always falls just before it.

genre/remote-control-hybride-orkest-en-e.text: Hans Zimmer came out of the European pop world and at first worked mainly with synthesizers. After Rain Man (1988), he built a studio in Santa Monica with a team of composers, first called Media Ventures and later Remote Control Productions. The way of working resembles an atelier: Zimmer devises themes and tone colour, and his collaborators work out scenes. The sound combines orchestra, choir and electronics, with heavy percussion, ostinatos in the strings and simple chord sequences that grow steadily fuller. Crimson Tide (1995) and Gladiator (2000) set the tone. Zimmer wrote The Dark Knight (2008) together with James Newton Howard. Inception (2010) is built on slowed-down music by Édith Piaf. Composers such as Klaus Badelt, Harry Gregson-Williams and John Powell came out of this atelier.
genre/remote-control-hybride-orkest-en-e.listen: Notice the repeated pattern in the strings and how the music grows bigger not through new melodies but through layers, percussion and volume.

genre/rhythm-and-blues.text: After the Second World War, big bands were too expensive to tour with. Small line-ups with piano, electric guitar, bass, drums and one or two saxophones made loud, danceable music for an urban Black audience: rhythm and blues. Leiber and Stoller wrote Hound Dog for Big Mama Thornton in 1952; in 1953 the record spent seven weeks at number 1 in the R&B chart.
genre/rhythm-and-blues.listen: Hear how, in Hound Dog, Big Mama Thornton shows a man the door, raw and powerful.

genre/riot-grrrl.text: In the early 1990s, a feminist punk movement arose in Olympia, in the state of Washington: riot grrrl. Bands such as Bikini Kill and Bratmobile found the punk scene a man's world; singer Kathleen Hanna called out ‘girls to the front’. The bands made fanzines and released their records on small, independent labels.
genre/riot-grrrl.listen: Rebel Girl is kept simple: a few chords, a hard drum and a lyric to shout along to.

genre/ritme-als-motor-stravinsky-en-bart.text: Around 1910, rhythm became the engine of the new music. Igor Stravinsky's ballet music Le sacre du printemps caused a riot on 29 May 1913 at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, with harsh, irregular accents and pagan rituals on stage. The Hungarian Béla Bartók collected thousands of folk songs and, in Allegro barbaro (1911), pounded the piano as if it were a percussion instrument. Their rhythmic power continues to work its way into film, jazz and rock.
genre/ritme-als-motor-stravinsky-en-bart.listen: Hear how the strings in Les augures printaniers keep stamping the same chord, with accents in unexpected places.

genre/rock-in-het-nederlands.text: After Doe Maar, Dutch became the language of rock too. The Frank Boeijen Groep made new wave in their own language, De Dijk soul and rhythm and blues with horns, The Scene solid guitar rock and the Heideroosjes punk. They filled the new pop venues with an audience that knew the lyrics word for word.
genre/rock-in-het-nederlands.listen: In Mag het licht uit, hear how De Dijk uses the warmth of a soul ballad for a Dutch lyric.

genre/rock-n-roll.text: Rock 'n' roll grew out of rhythm and blues, with influences from jump blues, boogie-woogie, gospel and country. Its recognisable features are the backbeat on beats 2 and 4 and a guitar riff as the hook. Rocket 88 (1951) is often called the first rock 'n' roll record; Rock Around the Clock brought the style to the general public in 1955.
genre/rock-n-roll.listen: Notice the loud snare drum on 2 and 4 and, in Rocket 88, the distorted guitar from a broken speaker.

genre/rockabilly.text: Rockabilly is the fast, stripped-down variant of rock 'n' roll in which country and rhythm and blues come together. You recognise it by the slapback echo on the voice, which defined the sound of Sun Records in Memphis, the slapped double bass and the metallic twang of the guitar. Elvis Presley, Gene Vincent and Eddie Cochran were the idols of the rockers in England and the nozems in the Netherlands.
genre/rockabilly.listen: In That's All Right, hear the slapback echo and Bill Black's slapped double bass. In C'mon Everybody you hear the stop-time riff, in which the band falls silent and Cochran sings his line into that silence.

genre/romantiek.text: In Romanticism, music became the expression of personal feeling, of nature, dreams and longing. Franz Schubert wrote hundreds of songs for voice and piano; in Erlkönig (1815), the piano gallops like a horse beneath the father, the child and the deadly Erl-King. Frédéric Chopin and Robert Schumann wrote short piano pieces, each with its own atmosphere, such as Chopin's nocturnes and Schumann's Kinderszenen. The piano became the instrument of the drawing room and the concert hall.
genre/romantiek.listen: Hear how the piano in Erlkönig keeps playing the same fast, hammering notes, like the hooves of a horse in the night.

genre/romeinse-muziek.text: The Romans took over much music from the Greeks, but turned it into spectacle. In the theatre, at triumphal processions and in the arena, the straight tuba, the round horn called the cornu and the hydraulis sounded, an organ from Alexandria in which water kept the air under pressure. A mosaic from Zliten in Libya shows that trio at gladiator fights. No Roman music has survived in written form; what we hear are reconstructions on rebuilt instruments.
genre/romeinse-muziek.listen: This is a reconstruction by Synaulia on rebuilt Roman instruments, because real Roman notation does not exist. Hear which tone colours the makers chose for an arena full of spectators, and which instruments you recognise.

genre/salsa.text: Salsa is the name that emerged in New York in the late 1960s for the Afro-Cuban dance music of Puerto Rican and Cuban musicians. The label Fania, with Johnny Pacheco, Willie Colón, Héctor Lavoe and Celia Cruz, made salsa big in the 1970s. Its basis is the son, with the clave and the montuno, supplemented with trombones, jazz chords and lyrics about life in the barrio.
genre/salsa.listen: In El Cantante, hear the fixed clave pattern beneath the trombones and the free singing of Héctor Lavoe.

genre/samba.text: Samba arose in the Afro-Brazilian neighbourhoods of Rio de Janeiro; Pelo Telefone (1917) is regarded as the first recorded samba. The music is in 2/4 and is driven by percussion, and from the 1930s samba became the music of carnival and of the radio. In 1958, João Gilberto and Antônio Carlos Jobim made a soft, restrained version of it: bossa nova.
genre/samba.listen: In Aquarela do Brasil, hear the samba rhythm in the percussion, beneath a large orchestra.

genre/schlager.text: Schlager is the German word for a hit and became the name for melodious, sentimental popular songs in German and Dutch. In the 1950s and 1960s, the schlager dominated the German charts, with singers such as Freddy Quinn and later Udo Jürgens and Heino. Until the Neue Deutsche Welle, German-language pop music was mostly schlager, and in the Netherlands too, a Dutch lyric long sounded like schlager or cabaret almost by default.
genre/schlager.listen: In Griechischer Wein, hear the singalong melody, the large orchestra and the lyric full of homesickness.

genre/serialisme.text: After the Second World War, young composers wanted to start completely afresh. At the summer courses in Darmstadt, they heard Olivier Messiaen's Mode de valeurs et d'intensités (1949), in which every note has a fixed duration, dynamic and attack. Pierre Boulez and Karlheinz Stockhausen went even further in Structures and Kreuzspiel, organising in series not only the pitches but also rhythm and volume. The result sounds like a starry sky of separate points.
genre/serialisme.listen: Hear how every note in Mode de valeurs stands on its own, with its own length and loudness, with no melody you can sing along to.

genre/shashmaqam.text: Shashmaqam means ‘six maqams’: Buzruk, Rost, Navo, Dugoh, Segoh and Iroq. In the mid-eighteenth century this cycle took shape among court musicians in Bukhara, where Jewish musicians also played a major role. Each maqam has an instrumental part and a sung part, the nasr, set to Persian and Uzbek poetry. The long-necked lute, the tanbur, leads; the frame drum, the doira, keeps the rhythm. The knowledge is passed on orally from master to pupil.
genre/shashmaqam.listen: Ari Babakhanov and his ensemble play the beginning of maqam Rost, the sarakhbor. Follow the voice: how does it slowly build towards a climax, and what is the doira doing at that moment?

genre/singer-songwriters.text: Singer-songwriters wrote their own songs, sang them themselves and told, in the first person, about their own lives. Carole King moved from the Brill Building to Los Angeles; her Tapestry (1971) became one of the best-selling albums of the 1970s. Joni Mitchell tuned her guitar in dozens of open tunings.
genre/singer-songwriters.listen: In Big Yellow Taxi, hear the skipping guitar in open tuning beneath a lyric about the environment.

genre/ska-rocksteady-en-reggae.text: In Kingston, sound systems played American rhythm and blues; when those records became scarce, Jamaican producers began recording their own. In this way ska, rocksteady and, around 1968, reggae arose in succession, with drums and bass as the riddim and the skank of the guitar on 2 and 4. Bob Marley became one of the first world stars from what was then called the Third World, and producers such as King Tubby turned it into dub.
genre/ska-rocksteady-en-reggae.listen: In Stir It Up, hear the one drop: the bass drum falls on the third beat and the first beat is left empty.

genre/skiffle.text: In the mid-1950s, skiffle swept through Britain as a craze, with roots in American folk and blues; Lonnie Donegan had a hit with Rock Island Line in 1956. All you needed was a cheap guitar, a washboard and a tea-chest bass. Thousands of teenagers started a band this way, among them John Lennon with The Quarrymen.
genre/skiffle.listen: In Rock Island Line, hear the simple line-up and the racing tempo: music that anyone could copy.

genre/smooth-jazz.text: In the mid-1970s a softer variant of fusion emerged, which became enormously popular in the 1980s. Smooth jazz borrows from soul and funk: a relaxed groove, warm chords and a melody on saxophone, guitar or electric piano, with a polished production. George Benson and Grover Washington Jr. were well-known names.
genre/smooth-jazz.listen: In Just the Two of Us, hear the relaxed groove beneath the saxophone and the voice of Bill Withers.

genre/soefimuziek.text: After the death of the poet Rumi in 1273, his followers founded the Mevlevi order in Konya, known for the whirling dervishes. Their ceremony, the sema, is a prayer in motion: the dancers turn with the right hand raised to heaven and the left hand towards the earth. The most important instrument is the ney, a reed flute with a breathy, rustling sound, and Rumi opened his great poem with the lament of that flute. Elsewhere, too, Sufis sing themselves into rapture with repeated hymns of praise.
genre/soefimuziek.listen: In this taksim, hear how Kudsi Ergüner lets his breath sound along in the ney: that rustling is part of the tone.

genre/softrock-en-aor.text: From the late 1960s, radio stations on the FM band played whole album sides: album-oriented rock. Soft rock, with its polished production and strong vocal melodies, lay close to pop and was heard from the early 1970s with the Carpenters, Bread and James Taylor; Rumours (1977) by Fleetwood Mac became one of the best-selling albums ever. In the 1980s, AOR sounded smooth and polished, with Toto and the power ballads of Foreigner.
genre/softrock-en-aor.listen: In Africa, hear how drummer Jeff Porcaro plays a light, straight groove beneath layers of percussion.

genre/son.text: The son comes from the east of Cuba and became popular in Havana in the 1920s. It mixes Spanish song forms and the tres, a Cuban guitar, with African rhythms and percussion: bongos, maracas and the clave. A singer alternates with a chorus, and in the second section the band repeats a short pattern, the montuno. The mambo, salsa and a large part of Latin jazz grew out of the son.
genre/son.listen: In Chan Chan, hear the tres, the ticking of the clave and the chorus answering the singer.

genre/soul.text: Soul arose in the mid-1950s out of gospel, jazz and rhythm and blues. In 1954, Ray Charles took the step from church to the charts with I Got a Woman, set to the melody of a gospel song. Soul became the soundtrack of the civil rights movement; Aretha Franklin's Respect became a song for civil rights and women's rights at once.
genre/soul.listen: In Respect, notice the melisma and the call and response between Aretha and the backing singers, the form of the church service.

genre/soul-jazz.text: Soul jazz is hard bop with even more gospel and blues, and a groove that makes the audience move along. The sound is often defined by the Hammond organ, an electric organ with a rotating speaker. Jimmy Smith from Norristown near Philadelphia made records with it for Blue Note from 1956, played the bass lines himself with his left hand and pedals, and became the example for a whole generation. Organ trios played in bars in Black neighbourhoods of Philadelphia, Newark and Harlem. The alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley had a success in 1959 with This Here by his pianist Bobby Timmons, and the Ramsey Lewis trio reached the charts in 1965 with The 'In' Crowd. At the Montreux festival in 1969, Les McCann and Eddie Harris recorded Compared to What. Hip hop producers would later sample a great deal of soul jazz.
genre/soul-jazz.listen: Notice the organ: it plays chords, melody and bass at the same time.

genre/southern-hiphop-en-crunk.text: From the late 1980s, the southern United States also developed its own hip hop: Geto Boys in Houston, Three 6 Mafia in Memphis and OutKast in Atlanta, who made their debut in 1994. DJ Screw in Houston slowed records down to a syrupy sound, chopped and screwed. Around 2000, Lil Jon turned crunk into party music with shouted choruses and heavy 808 basses. Trap grew out of this southern hip hop.
genre/southern-hiphop-en-crunk.listen: In Get Low, hear the bare beat with the heavy 808, the shouted lines and the call to the crowd.

genre/southern-rock.text: In the southern United States, southern rock arose around 1970, with The Allman Brothers Band as forerunners. Lynyrd Skynyrd from Jacksonville, Florida, made Sweet Home Alabama (1974) as a reply to two songs by Neil Young. Thirty years later, Kings of Leon began in that vein and scored with Sex on Fire (2008).
genre/southern-rock.listen: Hear the D-C-G riff of Sweet Home Alabama: the C is the flattened seventh degree of D, and that gives the Mixolydian sound of blues and country.

genre/sovjetfilmmuziek.text: In the Soviet Union, leading concert composers wrote for film, which the state regarded as the most important art form. Dmitri Shostakovich began in 1929 with music for the silent film Novyi Vavilon and went on writing film scores all his life. Sergei Prokofiev composed Luitenant Kizje (1934) and worked closely with the director Sergei Eisenstein on Aleksandr Nevski (1938) and Ivan the Terrible. In Nevski, director and composer matched image and music precisely to one another. The sound is large and direct: choirs, massive brass and simple, strong melodies. A late high point was Shostakovich's music for Grigori Kozintsev's Hamlet (1964).
genre/sovjetfilmmuziek.listen: Notice the contrast between rough, dissonant blocks of sound and simple, song-like melodies that you remember at once.

genre/spaghettiwestern.text: From 1964, Italian directors made Westerns in Spain and Italy, cheaper and harder-edged than the American ones. Ennio Morricone, trained as a trumpeter and composer at the conservatoire in Rome, found a new sound for them. In Sergio Leone's Per un pugno di dollari (1964), he combined a whistled melody, electric guitar, whip cracks, bells and a male choir. Every sound was given its own role, almost like a character. In Il buono, il brutto, il cattivo (1966), the main theme imitates the howl of a coyote. Luis Bacalov and Riz Ortolani followed with title songs and fierce guitar themes. Quentin Tarantino later often quoted this music.
genre/spaghettiwestern.listen: Notice the unusual tone colours: flutes, electric guitar, voices and effects, each with a role of its own.

genre/spectralisme.text: In Paris in 1973, Gérard Grisey and Tristan Murail founded the ensemble L'Itinéraire and began to investigate sound itself. Grisey had a low E on a trombone analysed electronically and divided its overtones among eighteen instruments: this is how Partiels (1975) begins. A piece became the slow unfolding of a single sound. The Finnish composer Kaija Saariaho, who worked at the Paris research institute IRCAM, built on these ideas.
genre/spectralisme.listen: Hear how the ensemble in Partiels imitates a low trombone note and lets the overtones light up one by one.

genre/spirituals-en-gospel.text: Spirituals arose in the nineteenth century among enslaved African Americans in the southern United States; in the Black churches, gospel grew out of them in the 1920s and 1930s: polyphonic religious songs with call and response. From 1938, Sister Rosetta Tharpe recorded gospel songs with the rhythm and swing of jazz, and in the 1940s was already playing solos on an electric guitar. Through singers who learned to sing in church, gospel became one of the roots of soul.
genre/spirituals-en-gospel.listen: Strange Things Happening Every Day is a gospel song, but if you pay no attention to the words, you hear a driving piano and a guitar solo as in rhythm and blues.

genre/spirituele-jazz.text: In December 1964, John Coltrane recorded A Love Supreme with his quartet, a suite in four parts that he dedicated to God. The album appeared in 1965 on Impulse! and gave direction to what has come to be called spiritual jazz: music as prayer or meditation, with long modal improvisations, repeated bass lines and an intense, searching tone. After Coltrane's death in 1967, his widow Alice Coltrane and the saxophonist Pharoah Sanders continued the line. Alice Coltrane brought in harp and organ and influences from Indian music; in 1969, Sanders recorded The Creator Has a Master Plan, with the singer Leon Thomas. The label Strata-East, founded by musicians themselves in 1971, released much of this music. Around 2015, there was renewed interest thanks to Kamasi Washington and the new scene in London.
genre/spirituele-jazz.listen: Notice the repeated bass line: it stays the same while everything above it grows.

genre/stax-en-memphis-soul.text: In Memphis, Jim Stewart started the label Satellite in 1957; his sister Estelle Axton joined a year later, and from 1961 it was called Stax (STewart + AXton). Recording was done live in an old cinema, and the sound was rawer and more southern than Motown: a heavy bass, dry drums and the Memphis Horns. The house band Booker T. & the MG's consisted of Black and white musicians.
genre/stax-en-memphis-soul.listen: Green Onions is a 12-bar blues in F: hear the repeated figure on the Hammond organ and the sharp guitar chords against it.

genre/streamingpop.text: Streaming pop is pop made for the way people have listened since the 2010s: via Spotify, YouTube and TikTok. Songs have become shorter on average, often begin straight away with the hook and mix genres freely. In December 2018, Lil Nas X from Atlanta put Old Town Road online, on a beat he had bought for 30 dollars. The song became big via TikTok, where thousands of users made videos to it, and spent nineteen weeks at number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. The debate over whether it was country showed how genres blur in the streaming era.
genre/streamingpop.listen: Hear the banjo from country on top of a trap beat with deep 808 bass and rattling hi-hats.

genre/stride-piano.text: Stride is a piano style from Harlem, grown out of ragtime. The left hand ‘strides’: a low bass note on the first and third beats, a chord in the middle of the keyboard on the second and fourth. As a result, a pianist sounds like a complete band. Stride is faster and freer than ragtime and is improvised. Pianists played at rent parties, parties where visitors paid to help the host raise the rent, and challenged one another in cutting contests. James P. Johnson was regarded as the master; his Carolina Shout was a test piece that the young Duke Ellington learned from a piano roll. Fats Waller was his pupil, Willie 'The Lion' Smith his rival. In the 1930s, Art Tatum took the technique to an unprecedented speed and harmonic richness.
genre/stride-piano.listen: Listen only to the left hand: low, middle, low, middle, and at a fast tempo.

genre/studio-ghibli.text: Studio Ghibli was founded in 1985 by Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata, after the success of Kaze no tani no Naushika (1984). From that film onwards, Miyazaki worked with Joe Hisaishi. Hisaishi came from minimal music and writes clear melodies that often begin small on the piano and grow into a full orchestra. He combines Western Romanticism with Japanese scales. Tonari no Totoro (1988) was given cheerful children's songs. Mononoke-hime (1997) is grand and dark, with a mighty main theme. Sen to Chihiro no kamikakushi (2001) alternates waltz, jazz and melancholy piano. Ghibli also worked with other composers, such as the French harpist Cécile Corbel for Kari-gurashi no Arietti (2010). Silence and natural sounds are given a great deal of room in these films.
genre/studio-ghibli.listen: Notice how a simple piano melody slowly acquires more instruments, until the whole orchestra takes over the theme.

genre/superhelden-en-franchise-sound.text: Danny Elfman, singer of the band Oingo Boingo, wrote a dark, gothic march theme for Tim Burton's Batman (1989). That became the model for superhero music: one recognisable motif, big brass, choir and heavy percussion. Shirley Walker developed that sound for Batman: The Animated Series (1992) into full orchestral music for every episode. With the Marvel film series from 2008, the franchise sound became important: music has to remain recognisable across many films. For The Avengers (2012), Alan Silvestri wrote a fanfare that returns in later films. In Black Panther (2018), Ludwig Göransson combined a Western orchestra with Senegalese singing and African drums, and won an Oscar for it. Pinar Toprak wrote the music for Captain Marvel (2019).
genre/superhelden-en-franchise-sound.listen: Listen to the main motif: how many notes does it have, which instrument plays it, and at what moment does it return when the hero springs into action?

genre/surfrock.text: In the early 1960s, young musicians in Southern California made surf rock: instrumental guitar music with plenty of reverb, in which fast, repeated notes imitate the roar of the waves. In Misirlou (1962), Dick Dale played an old Middle Eastern melody in that way. The Beach Boys turned it into vocal music, with multi-part harmonies; Brian Wilson later developed from this the studio records with which he challenged The Beatles.
genre/surfrock.listen: In Misirlou, hear the reverberating guitar and the fast, repeated notes on a single string.

genre/suspense-en-psychologische-thrille.text: Between 1955 and 1964, Alfred Hitchcock and Bernard Herrmann collaborated on a series of films. Herrmann, born in New York and also a conductor, thought in short motifs rather than long melodies. He repeated small cells, left harmonies unresolved and chose unusual instrumentations. In Vertigo (1958), spiralling arpeggios circle around, like the dizziness of the main character. In Psycho (1960), he used only strings, with the shrill, stabbing chords of the shower scene. This work laid the foundation for modern thriller music. In the Hitchcockian thriller Charade (1963), Henry Mancini showed how suspense goes together with an elegant, lighter theme.
genre/suspense-en-psychologische-thrille.listen: Notice short, repeated motifs and chords that do not resolve, so that the tension lingers.

genre/sutartines.text: In Aukštaitija, in the north-east of Lithuania, women sang sutartinės even before the Christianisation of the country, named after the verb sutarti: ‘to agree’. Two or three female singers sing short melodies that constantly cross one another, often in a tight canon. Where the voices clash, seconds are heard, which are regarded here as pleasing. The texts are about work, weddings and the seasons. UNESCO recognised this centuries-old tradition in 2010.
genre/sutartines.listen: The trio Trys Keturiose sings a sutartinė about a little bee and clover. Try to follow one voice and hear how the others rub over and against it. How often do you hear two voices right next to each other?

genre/swing-en-big-band.text: In the 1930s, the New Orleans band grew into the big band of twelve to seventeen musicians, with an arranger who wrote riffs for the sections. The eighth notes are played long-short and the bass walks on all four beats. Duke Ellington led the orchestra of the Cotton Club in Harlem; the white Benny Goodman became the ‘King of Swing’.
genre/swing-en-big-band.listen: In Take the 'A' Train, hear the AABA form and how saxophones and brass answer one another.

genre/symfonische-metal.text: Symphonic metal combines heavy guitars and drums with orchestral sounds, choirs and a classically trained voice. The Netherlands became a centre of the style: Within Temptation, founded in 1996 around the singer Sharon den Adel, and Epica, founded in 2002, play at festivals all over the world.
genre/symfonische-metal.listen: In Mother Earth, hear how orchestra and choir rise above the distorted guitars, with the clear voice of Sharon den Adel.

genre/symfonische-rock.text: Symphonic rock brought classical music into pop: orchestras, church organ, Mellotron and themes by Bach or Beethoven. The organ part of Procol Harum's A Whiter Shade of Pale (1967) is inspired by Bach, and The Moody Blues recorded Days of Future Passed (1967) with an orchestra. In the Netherlands, Ekseption played Beethoven's Fifth as a rock song, and groups such as Focus and Kayak made symphonic rock a Dutch speciality.
genre/symfonische-rock.listen: In A Whiter Shade of Pale, hear how the Hammond organ plays a melody that sounds like Baroque music, while the bass walks step by step downwards.

genre/symfonische-stommefilmscore-hollyw.text: Around 1915, major premieres were given a full orchestra with a specially compiled or composed score. For the racist epic The Birth of a Nation (1915), Joseph Carl Breil made a mixture of his own themes, folk songs and classical quotations, such as Wagner's Ride of the Valkyries. In Berlin in 1926, Edmund Meisel wrote harsh, rhythmic music for Eisenstein's Battleship Potemkin, which followed the editing shot by shot. Gottfried Huppertz composed a large late-Romantic work for Metropolis (1927), with leitmotifs for the characters and the world of the machines. These scores showed that film music could be a coherent symphonic whole. Hollywood adopted that model in the 1930s.
genre/symfonische-stommefilmscore-hollyw.listen: Notice how the music follows the editing: short, hammering rhythms in Meisel, recurring leitmotifs in Huppertz.

genre/symfonische-terugkeer-williams-tij.text: In the 1960s, the large orchestra partly disappeared from Hollywood, in favour of pop and jazz. John Williams brought it back. For Jaws (1975), a menacing two-note motif in the low strings was enough. He recorded Star Wars (1977) with the London Symphony Orchestra, in the style of Korngold and with leitmotifs as Wagner used them: every character and every idea gets a theme of its own. Superman (1978) and E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) followed. Other composers joined in, such as Alan Silvestri with Back to the Future (1985) and James Horner. This is how the blockbuster sound came about: brass fanfares, broad string melodies and music that plays along almost continuously. That approach defines the adventure film to this day.
genre/symfonische-terugkeer-williams-tij.listen: Follow one leitmotif through an excerpt: notice when it sounds in the brass, when softly in the strings, and how it changes character.

genre/synthdisco-en-hi-nrg.text: In Munich in 1977, the producer Giorgio Moroder made I Feel Love with Donna Summer, without a band: the bass line comes from a Moog driven by a sequencer. The song stands at the beginning of Hi-NRG, Italo disco and later house. Hi-NRG itself took shape in the early 1980s in gay clubs in San Francisco, New York and London: fast, electronic dance music, with producers such as Patrick Cowley and Bobby Orlando.
genre/synthdisco-en-hi-nrg.listen: Hear the bass line that a sequencer repeats endlessly and exactly in time, with the high, long-held singing above it.

genre/synthesizerorkest-ambient-en-new-a.text: Jean-Michel Jarre, who had worked with Pierre Schaeffer, recorded Oxygène in 1976 in a home studio in Paris. From London, Vangelis made film music such as Chariots of Fire, and in Japan Kitaro made music without a beat for the series Silk Road. Tangerine Dream and Klaus Schulze in Berlin had preceded them, and in 1978 Brian Eno gave the genre its name, ambient, with Music for Airports.
genre/synthesizerorkest-ambient-en-new-a.listen: In Oxygène, hear the cheap Korg rhythm box beneath simple melodies that stick in the mind.

genre/synthpop.text: Synth-pop is the most poppy branch of new wave: Kraftwerk was the example for Gary Numan, OMD and The Human League, and later for the Pet Shop Boys. Often it is a duo of a singer and someone behind the synthesizers. Eurythmics recorded Sweet Dreams largely by themselves, in an attic studio in north London, with a drum machine that also drove the bass line, and Bronski Beat sang openly about life as gay men.
genre/synthpop.listen: In Tainted Love, hear how a soul song from 1964 is given a cold, electronic version.

genre/synthwave.text: Synthwave is electronic music that imitates the sound of the 1980s: analogue synthesizers, reverberant drums, arpeggios from Italo disco and images of neon and old films. French producers such as Kavinsky and College made it popular in the mid-2000s; Nightcall (2010) was heard in the film Drive (2011). The Weeknd, too, used those sounds in Blinding Lights.
genre/synthwave.listen: In Nightcall, hear the slow beat, the distorted voice and the synthesizers that recall the 1980s.

genre/synthwave-revival.text: Around 2010, musicians reached back to the synthesizer sound of the 1980s, with soft washes of sound, arpeggios and drum machines. Nicolas Winding Refn's Drive (2011) brought that style to the cinema with a score by Cliff Martinez, former drummer of the Red Hot Chili Peppers, supplemented with songs by Kavinsky and College, among others. Disasterpeace, who had previously made music for games, wrote a hard synthesizer score for the horror film It Follows (2014) in the spirit of John Carpenter. Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein of the band S U R V I V E made the title music for the series Stranger Things (2016). Nostalgia and a warm, analogue sound are characteristic.
genre/synthwave-revival.listen: Notice the arpeggios of analogue synthesizers and the warm, hazy layer of sound beneath them.

genre/tamil-en-zuid-indiase-filmmuziek.text: In Chennai, Tamil cinema developed a musical tradition of its own. Ilaiyaraaja made his debut in 1976 with Annakkili. He mixed Tamil folk music with Western classical harmony, which he had studied thoroughly, and wrote music for more than a thousand films. For Mani Ratnam's Nayakan (1987), he also sang himself. A.R. Rahman, who had previously made advertising jingles, made his debut in 1992 with Roja, also by Mani Ratnam. He worked with synthesizers, a studio of his own and new voices, and made the sound fuller and more modern. After Bombay (1995), he became known throughout India, and later internationally too, with an Oscar for Slumdog Millionaire.
genre/tamil-en-zuid-indiase-filmmuziek.listen: Notice how folk melodies and rhythms combine with Western harmonies, strings and synthesizers.

genre/tango.text: Tango arose in the late nineteenth century in the port districts of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, where European immigrants, Afro-Argentines and people from the countryside came together. The rhythm has its roots in the habanera, and the bandoneón, a concertina-type accordion from Germany, became the principal instrument. The singer Carlos Gardel made tango world-famous in the 1920s and 1930s; from the 1950s, Astor Piazzolla renewed it with influences from jazz and classical music.
genre/tango.listen: In Por una Cabeza, hear the bandoneón and the violins, and the rhythm that keeps pausing briefly and then pressing on again.

genre/tarab-de-egyptische-gouden-eeuw.text: Tarab is the Arabic word for the rapture that music evokes in listeners. In Cairo, that rapture became mass culture: from the 1930s, Umm Kulthum gave a concert on the first Thursday of every month that was broadcast live on the radio, and then the streets stayed empty. She sang lines again and again and differently each time, encouraged by the hall, so that a single song could last an hour. In Anta Oumri (1964), her first song by Mohammed Abdel Wahab, even an electric guitar can be heard.
genre/tarab-de-egyptische-gouden-eeuw.listen: In Anta Oumri, listen to the orchestra: strings, oud and qanun play one melody together, each with small ornaments of its own.

genre/thaise-piphat.text: The piphat is the most important ensemble of Thai classical music, related to the Cambodian pinpeat. In the kingdom of Ayutthaya, founded in 1351, melodic percussion instruments such as the xylophone ranat ek and the gong circle khong wong acquired a fixed place. The shawm pi nai plays a richly ornamented melody, while drums and small cymbals keep the beat. Piphat is heard at Buddhist ceremonies and at the masked dance theatre khon.
genre/thaise-piphat.listen: Fong Naam opens with Sathukarn, the prayer with which a piphat performance begins. Hear how the instruments play the same melody at the same time, but each in its own way. Which instrument sounds highest and fastest?

genre/theremin-tape-en-elektronische-pio.text: Electronic sounds came into film by way of the theremin, an instrument that you play without touching it. Shostakovich had already used it in 1931 in the Soviet film Odna, but in Hollywood the instrument only broke through in the 1940s. Miklós Rózsa used it in Spellbound (1945) for the troubled mind of the main character. In The Day the Earth Stood Still (1951), Bernard Herrmann placed two theremins alongside electric violin, bass and guitar. For Forbidden Planet (1956), Bebe and Louis Barron made an entirely electronic soundtrack with self-built circuits; the end credits speak of ‘electronic tonalities’. In London in 1963, Delia Derbyshire realised the Doctor Who theme with tape. Eduard Artemyev used the ANS synthesizer for Solaris (1972).
genre/theremin-tape-en-elektronische-pio.listen: Notice the floating, gliding sound of the theremin and sounds that do not imitate any existing instrument.

genre/third-stream.text: Third stream is the name that the composer and horn player Gunther Schuller gave in 1957 to music that brings jazz and classical music together: a third current alongside the two main streams. It is not about jazz with strings added, but about pieces in which improvisation and compositional techniques from classical music, such as the fugue, genuinely work together. On the 1956 record Music for Brass, a brass ensemble played work by Schuller, John Lewis, J.J. Johnson and Jimmy Giuffre, with Miles Davis as soloist. For the jazz festival of Brandeis University in 1957, Charles Mingus and George Russell, among others, wrote new pieces. John Lewis's Modern Jazz Quartet brought fugues and Baroque forms into a jazz quartet. Schuller continued to defend the movement, among other things as president of the New England Conservatory in Boston.
genre/third-stream.listen: Hear where the piece sounds written out and where the players improvise freely.

genre/tin-pan-alley.text: From about 1885, music publishers settled close together in Manhattan, from the 1890s mainly on West 28th Street. Songwriters wrote songs, publishers sold them as sheet music and song pluggers played them; from the 1920s, the 32-bar song in AABA form became the standard. Irving Berlin, George Gershwin and Cole Porter were the big names.
genre/tin-pan-alley.listen: In White Christmas, hear how Bing Crosby sings softly and close by, thanks to the microphone: crooning.

extra.text: Around 1900, dozens of music publishers in New York were housed in the same stretch of street: West 28th Street, between Fifth and Sixth Avenue. Every office had a piano, on which new songs were tried out all day long. On warm days, that sounded through the open windows like someone banging on pots and pans. That is how the street got the nickname Tin Pan Alley. Writing songs became a profession here, with an office and a deadline.

genre/toeval-en-stilte-john-cage.text: At first John Cage prepared the piano with screws and rubber; from 1951 he let chance take part in the composing and determined notes, durations and volumes with the Chinese oracle book I Ching. In Imaginary Landscape No. 4, twelve radios play, and what is heard depends on that evening's broadcasts. In 1952, in 4'33", the pianist David Tudor sat silently at the grand piano for more than four minutes, so that the sounds in the hall became the music.
genre/toeval-en-stilte-john-cage.listen: In Imaginary Landscape No. 4, hear how scraps of radio voices, music and noise alternate by chance.

genre/trailermuziek-en-epic-music.text: A trailer has to sell a whole film in two minutes. Often the film music is not yet ready, so specialised companies make their own trailer music. Two Steps from Hell, founded in 2006 by Thomas Bergersen and Nick Phoenix, at first supplied only film studios. Such pieces usually follow a fixed form in three parts: a quiet opening, a build-up with percussion and ostinato, and a big finale with choir and orchestra. Around the trailers for Inception (2010), the low, metallic ‘braam’ sound became a cliché. Zack Hemsey wrote ‘Mind Heist’ for the third Inception trailer. Later, these makers released their music on albums for a wide audience. In this way epic music grew into a genre in its own right, with its own fans and concerts.
genre/trailermuziek-en-epic-music.listen: Follow the form in three steps: quiet opening, build-up with drums and repeated figures, and a climax in which choir and brass give everything at once.

genre/trance.text: Trance arose around 1990 in Germany, above all in Frankfurt and Berlin: electronic dance music with long build-ups, floating synthesizer chords and melodies that keep returning. The Age of Love (1990) is regarded as one of the first tracks. DJs such as Sven Väth and Paul van Dyk made the genre big, and in the late 1990s trance became an export product in the Netherlands.
genre/trance.listen: In For an Angel, hear the arpeggios that keep building towards the moment when the melody comes in fully.

genre/trap.text: In Atlanta from the early 2000s, trap grew, a hip hop style from the southern United States, named after the trap house where drugs were sold. T.I., Young Jeezy and Gucci Mane were the first names. Its basis is long, gliding 808 bass drums and fast hi-hat rolls, and Auto-Tune became an ordinary part of the voice. Old Town Road (2018) showed how trap could mix with country.
genre/trap.listen: In What You Know, hear the deep 808 bass and the hi-hats rattling in fast rolls.

genre/triphop.text: Trip hop is a form of downtempo from the producer scene of Bristol, where sound systems played reggae, hip hop, soul and punk all mixed together. Massive Attack emerged from the collective The Wild Bunch. Slow, heavy breakbeats, samples of old records, a deep reggae bass and singing that is more atmosphere than story.
genre/triphop.listen: In Unfinished Sympathy, hear the slow beat beneath strings and a voice that creates atmosphere.

genre/troubadours-en-trouveres.text: William IX, Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitiers, is the oldest troubadour whose poems have survived; he lived from 1071 to 1126. Troubadours composed and sang in Occitan, the vernacular of southern France, and not in the Latin of the church. Their great theme was courtly love for an unattainable lady. In northern France, the trouvères followed in Old French, and with them the European love song begins.
genre/troubadours-en-trouveres.listen: In this song by Bernart de Ventadorn, about a lark flying up into the sunlight, hear how every verse is sung to the same melody, so that the text gets all the attention.

genre/uk-garage.text: In the late 1990s, London DJs and producers turned American garage and house into a style of their own, faster and with influences from jungle: UK garage, and later 2-step, with a skipping rhythm in which the bass drum does not fall on every beat. Pirate radio and clubs played it, and Craig David scored with Artful Dodger with Re-Rewind (1999). Grime and dubstep grew out of UK garage.
genre/uk-garage.listen: In Re-Rewind, hear the skipping 2-step rhythm, the deep bass and the smooth singing of Craig David.

genre/vaporwave.text: Vaporwave arose around 2010 on the internet. As Chuck Person, Daniel Lopatin slowed down snippets of 1980s pop songs and let them repeat endlessly. In December 2011, Ramona Xavier released the album Floral Shoppe as Macintosh Plus, full of slowed-down soul, lift music and advertising jingles. The name refers to vaporware: software that is announced but never appears. Vaporwave plays with the feel of old computers, shopping malls and adverts, and is half joke, half criticism of consumer society.
genre/vaporwave.listen: In Lisa Frank 420 / Modern Computing, hear how a slowed-down snippet of Diana Ross's It's Your Move keeps starting over, as if the record is stuck.

genre/vedische-zang.text: Around 1500 BCE, the hymns of the Rigveda arose in the north-west of India, in the region of the Punjab. Brahmins learned them by heart with clever methods of practice, in which they repeated the words in constantly different orders. In this way, text and pitch remained virtually unchanged for well over three thousand years, without being written down. The Samaveda sets the hymns to melodies and is regarded as a root of Indian music.
genre/vedische-zang.listen: In this recitation of the Rigveda, hear how the voice stays on a few pitches, with small rises and falls that belong to the text. Then compare it with the Samaveda, where the text is truly sung.

genre/venetiaanse-meerkorigheid.text: In San Marco in Venice, singers and musicians stood facing one another on different galleries. Adriaan Willaert from Flanders, choirmaster from 1527, wrote psalms for two choirs that alternate. Andrea and Giovanni Gabrieli developed that into music for several choirs with cornetts, trombones and violins. Giovanni's Sonata pian' e forte of 1597 contains one of the first instances of loud and soft written into the notes, and that play with space and sound pointed forward to the Baroque.
genre/venetiaanse-meerkorigheid.listen: In Andrea Gabrieli's Gloria for sixteen voices, hear how groups of singers and wind players alternate, as if they sound from different sides of the church, and only play all together at the high points.

genre/verbunkos-en-roma-orkesten.text: After 1715, the imperial army lured young men into service in Hungarian inns with drink, dance and music. From that recruitment, in German Werbung, grew the verbunkos, a name that appears in the 1770s. A slow section with dotted rhythms, the lassú, is followed by a fast and virtuosic section, the friss. Roma violinists such as János Bihari made the style famous. Liszt, Brahms and later Bartók incorporated it into their own work.
genre/verbunkos-en-roma-orkesten.listen: Here Bartók himself plays piano, with the violinist Joseph Szigeti and the clarinettist Benny Goodman, in the first movement of his Contrasts, which he called Verbunkos. Can you hear the dotted rhythms and the proud, stately gait of the old recruiting dance?

genre/vocale-jazz.text: Jazz singing begins with the blues singers and with Louis Armstrong, who in 1926 scatted on Heebie Jeebies: improvising with sounds without words. Billie Holiday sang just behind the beat and altered melodies towards her own speech. Ella Fitzgerald combined a clear timbre with virtuosic scat and, between 1956 and 1964, recorded a series of songbooks for Verve with songs by Cole Porter, Duke Ellington, George Gershwin and others. Sarah Vaughan brought the harmonies of bebop into her singing. In vocalese, singers set words to existing instrumental solos; Lambert, Hendricks & Ross made it their speciality. Most jazz singers draw on the Great American Songbook, the songs from Broadway musicals and films. In the Netherlands, Rita Reys and Ann Burton became known; today, singers include Cécile McLorin Salvant and Samara Joy.
genre/vocale-jazz.listen: Notice how the singer plays with the beat: just too late, just too early, and yet always back on time.

genre/vroege-geluidsfilm-talkies.text: With The Jazz Singer (1927), synchronised sound came to the cinema. Warner Bros. used the Vitaphone system: the sound was on large discs that ran in sync with the film. Al Jolson sang a handful of songs and spoke a few sentences. In the first years, everything revolved around singing. Musicals such as The Broadway Melody (1929) put new hits on the market. Continuous background music was difficult, because recording and mixing were still cumbersome. Music therefore sounded mainly when it had a source on screen, such as a singer or an orchestra. In Europe, René Clair (Sous les toits de Paris) and Josef von Sternberg (Der blaue Engel, 1930) made the song the core of the story.
genre/vroege-geluidsfilm-talkies.listen: Listen to the sound of the early recording technique and note that the music almost always comes from a singer or orchestra on screen.

genre/vroege-hiphop.text: On 11 August 1973, Kool Herc, who knew the sound systems of Kingston, DJed at a party on Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx. With two copies of the same record, he extended the break, and MCs began to rap over it. The first rap hit was Rapper's Delight (1979); The Message (1982) was the first rap hit to describe life in the ghetto.
genre/vroege-hiphop.listen: In The Message, hear the slow tempo, the menacing mood and the synthesizer line that keeps returning.

genre/vroege-opera.text: Around 1600, scholars and musicians in Florence wanted to revive Greek drama, with a single voice above a simple accompaniment instead of four voices intertwined. This is how opera arose: Jacopo Peri's Euridice sounded in 1600 in the Palazzo Pitti at a princely wedding. In 1607 in Mantua, Claudio Monteverdi turned it into full-fledged music theatre with L'Orfeo, with orchestra, choruses and arias. From 1637, public opera houses in Venice drew paying audiences.
genre/vroege-opera.listen: In the Toccata, hear how the trumpets play a festive fanfare above a single long-held bass note.
